1.pericope_label: And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not. And there went out fire from the Lord, and devoured them, and they died before the Lord.

schools.summary: Itemise the offence into four transgressions — a private censer, two men where one was appointed, an encroachment on the high priest's sole right to burn incense in a censer, and an unauthorised hour — and read the reversal in the fire itself, since what came out to consume the sacrifices as a token of acceptance now comes out to consume the sacrificers; then infer from the bodies being carried out in their coats that the fire slew without burning.

Defend the severity without pretending the offence looks grave: their thoughtlessness would seem excusable, since they set about a novelty too eagerly and were led into error by their own precipitancy, and the punishment will not please those who superciliously criticise God's judgments — but religion had to be sanctioned at its very commencement, since impunity for Aaron's own sons would have taught the whole Law to be neglected.

Supply what the text assumes, the whole procedure of burning incense as the Jewish sources describe it, down to the weight burnt morning and evening and the people withdrawing from between the porch and the altar; then join it to the priest in the gospel whose incense burnt while the multitude prayed outside, and draw the lesson that a High Priest adds incense to his people's prayers.

Ask the prior question, whether they had any business burning incense at all that day, since the whole service of the inauguration was Aaron's and his sons were only to attend him — so that pride in a new honour and ambition for its most honourable part drove them to act without orders and with common incense.

sides.position: Four transgressions in one act: a private censer, two men where one was appointed, encroachment on the high priest's sole right, and an unauthorised hour
Burning incense at all that day without orders, the whole service belonging to Aaron, and so with common incense from a strange fire
Simply using fire not taken from the altar, which the law implicitly forbade

outliers.note: Alone reproduces the whole Jewish procedure for burning incense, down to the hundred denaries burnt daily and the people withdrawing from between the porch and the altar, and joins it to Zacharias in the gospel.

3.pericope_label: Then Moses said unto Aaron, This is it that the Lord spake, saying, I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified. And Aaron held his peace.

schools.summary: Say flatly that we seek in vain for the words referred to, canvass the passages proposed and report the objection that men who call it spoken-but-unwritten do so to gain some show for their own unwritten traditions; paraphrase the saying as a chain, that when God is sanctified by the priests of highest dignity his glory shines before the whole people; and note that punishing obscure persons teaches little where punishing the illustrious draws all eyes.

Render the silence literally — and Aaron was dumb — and ask how elegantly expressive it is of parental affection, of his sense of his sons' presumption and of his submission to God's justice, with Seneca's line for it, that slight sorrows are loquacious while deep anguish has no voice; and lay out both senses of the saying, the duty of sanctifying God and God's purpose of sanctifying himself.

Call the quoted saying a reference to a divine communication not previously written down, and make both verbs reflexive: God sanctified Aaron's sons by the holy unction that they might sanctify him by strict performance, and having failed, he sanctified himself in them by the punishment; then hear the psalmist behind the silence, I was dumb, I opened not my mouth, because thou didst it.

Admire the composure of Moses rather than the silence of Aaron, a brother born for adversity who kept decorum in the sanctuary when every face gathered blackness; and turn the priesthood on the reader, since in worship we all come nigh to God as spiritual priests.

debates.question: Where had God spoken the words Moses quotes?

sides.position: Nowhere on record: it is a divine communication not previously written down in the Pentateuch
Not in these words, but in substance at the charge to the priests who come near to sanctify themselves, and in the whole tenour of the law
At the consecration charge, keep ye the Lord's charge that ye die not
At one or another passage in Exodus
Spoken but not written, as many things beside — an answer suspected of serving a case for unwritten traditions
Probably uttered by Moses in God's name though unrecorded, since Scripture gives only the heads of discourses

debates.question: Does “I will be sanctified” state a duty or a purpose?

sides.position: Either: their duty to sanctify God, or God's purpose to sanctify himself by impartial punishment
God's purpose, both verbs being reflexive: having failed to sanctify him, they were made the means of his sanctifying himself

outliers.note: Alone explains the silence physiologically, that excessive grief stupefies the mind so that amazement prevents both tears and complaints, and quotes Seneca — slight sorrows are loquacious, deep anguish has no voice.
Alone reports the suspicion that those who call the saying spoken-but-unwritten do so in order to gain some show for their own unwritten traditions.

themes: sanctified in them that come nigh

4.pericope_label: And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said unto them, Come near, carry your brethren from before the sanctuary out of the camp. So they went near, and carried them in their coats out of the camp; as Moses had said. And Moses said unto Aaron, and unto Eleazar and unto Ithamar, his sons, Uncover not your heads, neither rend your clothes; lest ye die, and lest wrath come upon all the people: but let your brethren, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning which the Lord hath kindled. And ye shall not go out from the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, lest ye die: for the anointing oil of the Lord is upon you. And they did according to the word of Moses.

schools.summary: Ask why these particular cousins were summoned and answer from what came later, since the children of the elder uncles had already begun the discontent that broke out in Korah's rebellion, and men who suffered for transgressing a divine institution had to be buried by men of unimpeachable allegiance; render the coats tunics and explain that priestly cast-offs ordinarily became lamp-wick; and insist the head was not uncovered but dishevelled, its growth uncut.
Give the plain motive, that Eleazar and Ithamar were not to pollute themselves by carrying the bodies, and allow that all present may simply have been stupefied by terror.

Offer two readings of the burial in the holy garments without choosing — a testimony of respect still due, God remembering mercy in judgment; or garments polluted by the sin and by the touch of the dead and so never to be used again — and give sanitary and ceremonial reasons together for burial outside the camp; then turn the whole into an attack on burying the dead within towns, and within places dedicated to worship, as an abomination at which piety and common sense shudder.

debates.question: Why were Mishael and Elzaphan chosen rather than nearer kin?

sides.position: Because the elder uncles' children had already begun the discontent that became Korah's rebellion, and the buriers had to be of unimpeachable allegiance
Because Eleazar and Ithamar would have polluted themselves by carrying the bodies
Because Aaron and his sons were engaged in ministrations from which they were not called away for funerals

debates.question: Why were the bodies buried in the priestly garments?

sides.position: As a testimony of the respect still due the men, God remembering mercy in judgment
Because the garments were polluted by the sin and by the touch of the dead, and were never to be used again
Because nobody would have used garments worn at so awful a visitation, though they were ordinarily made into lamp-wick

outliers.note: Alone connects the choice of buriers with the later rebellion of Korah, arguing that the discontent of the elder uncles’ children had already begun to show itself.
Alone turns the burial outside the camp into an attack on burying the dead within towns and within places dedicated to worship.

8.pericope_label: And the Lord spake unto Aaron, saying, Do not drink wine nor strong drink, thou, nor thy sons with thee, when ye go into the tabernacle of the congregation, lest ye die: it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations: And that ye may put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean; And that ye may teach the children of Israel all the statutes which the Lord hath spoken unto them by the hand of Moses.

schools.summary: Read the direct address to Aaron as consolation and repair, half the priesthood struck down and the people needing the office's prestige restored; date the drunkenness theory to at least the time of Christ and cite the Chaldee's outright gloss; and enter the distinction the law requires, that common is a wider notion than unclean, everything counting as common that is not fitted for the sanctuary.

Report the Jewish explanations of why God addressed Aaron and prefer the plain one, that he was now high priest in the execution of his office; reconstruct the feast on the peace offerings that may lie behind the prohibition; and correct Jerome's definition of strong drink, restricting it to liquors expressed from fruits, in whose sweetness there is nearly as much to tempt men as in wine.

Trace the second term to a root meaning to inebriate, cover any fermented liquor by it, and follow it through Jerome and a Mohammedan Indian drink to our own word cider; call the drunkenness theory not improbable while resting nothing on it; and note that the devil, being God's ape, required the same abstinence of his own priests.

Find a delicate reason for the direct address, that the caution might have been taken amiss from Moses as though he suspected his brother of being a wine-bibber, since we are so apt to resent cautions as accusations; and limit the ban to the time of ministration, drunkenness being bad in any man but especially scandalous in ministers, who ought of all men to have the clearest heads.

sides.position: The placing of the law gives the suspicion real force, and they had feasted that day on the peace offerings
So the cabalistical commentators held, and the opinion was current at least as early as the time of Christ
Not improbable, but nothing rests on it, since drunkenness in a minister is reason enough for the law
The occasion of the law lies in the event, but the further inference is not to be drawn
Against it: Scripture nowhere states it, and the offenders had been ministering since early morning

outliers.note: Alone observes that the devil, being God’s ape, required the same abstinence of his own priests in their idolatrous service.
Alone traces the word for strong drink through Jerome and a prohibited Mohammedan drink in India, and suggests that our own word cider descends from it.

12.pericope_label: And Moses spake unto Aaron, and unto Eleazar and unto Ithamar, his sons that were left, Take the meat offering that remaineth of the offerings of the Lord made by fire, and eat it without leaven beside the altar: for it is most holy: And ye shall eat it in the holy place, because it is thy due, and thy sons’ due, of the sacrifices of the Lord made by fire: for so I am commanded. And the wave breast and heave shoulder shall ye eat in a clean place; thou, and thy sons, and thy daughters with thee: for they be thy due, and thy sons’ due, which are given out of the sacrifices of peace offerings of the children of Israel. The heave shoulder and the wave breast shall they bring with the offerings made by fire of the fat, to wave it for a wave offering before the Lord; and it shall be thine, and thy sons’ with thee, by a statute for ever; as the Lord hath commanded.

schools.summary: Give the psychological reason for the repetition, that men little practised in the rites and confounded by consternation could not apply themselves with composure, so the offering would have been improperly made; and notice what the reason given does, setting before them the authority of God, on which the priesthood is founded and to which it ought to be subject.

Add the second motive, that grief-driven abstinence would have been at once a signification of the forbidden sorrow and a fresh transgression; locate the eating exactly, in the court near the altar of burnt offerings; and draw out the consequence of the lower grade, that these portions might be eaten where the women came as well as the men, a priest's daughters eating them as well as his sons.

Explain the anxiety behind the repetition, that a house which had just lost two sons for violating the sacrificial rules must be guarded against transgressing any other part of them; set out what most holy entailed, eating beside the altar within the court and by the male members of the priestly families only; and render the phrase a holy place rather than the holy place.

Draw the principle from the resumption itself, that afflictions should quicken us to duty rather than take us off from it, and read the phrase about the sons that were left both ways — comfort to the father who was spared two, and an engagement on the two spared to fill the places of the gone by double diligence; then make the passage a second lesson in discrimination, between the most holy and the merely holy.

debates.question: Where was the meat offering to be eaten?

sides.position: In a holy place, meaning any part of the sacred court, not the holy place properly so called
In the court, near the altar of burnt offerings

outliers.note: Alone draws out that the lighter holy things could be eaten wherever the women came as well as the men, a priest’s daughters eating them as well as his sons, whether maids, widows or divorced.

themes: the wave breast and heave shoulder

16.pericope_label: And Moses diligently sought the goat of the sin offering, and, behold, it was burnt: and he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron which were left alive, saying, Wherefore have ye not eaten the sin offering in the holy place, seeing it is most holy, and God hath given it you to bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the Lord? Behold, the blood of it was not brought in within the holy place: ye should indeed have eaten it in the holy place, as I commanded.

schools.summary: Turn the incident into a lesson about teaching, since Moses had told them what to do and his own sacrifice was a visible instruction enough even for children, yet they perverted it as if they had neither heard nor seen anything — whence the ablest teacher's work is fruitless without obedient scholars of retentive memory; and survey the rabbinic accounts of how many goats were offered that day before choosing among them.

State plainly what happened, that the confusion following the death of Nadab and Abihu led to the goat being burnt instead of eaten; catch the edge in the phrase about the sons left alive, who of all men ought to have taken warning; and give the milder account of the priest's portion, a reward of service by which the people's sins are taken away in the sacrifices through which God is reconciled to penitent offerers.

Identify the goat as the people's sin offering of the eighth day and supply the motive for burning it, that men overwhelmed with grief could not eat while none but priests might partake; explain why the anger spared the father, whose duty it equally was; and weigh the rendering of bearing the iniquity against removing it, reporting the versions on one side and the Vulgate and the Reformers on the other.

sides.position: The people's sin offering of that day, the only one certainly offered
The goat of the new moon, the only one of the three that was burnt
The one always to be offered, not a temporary affair like the others

debates.question: Does “bear the iniquity of the congregation” mean bear or remove?

sides.position: Remove or bear away, as the Septuagint, Chaldee and Syriac render it
Bear, with the Vulgate and the Reformers: the priest by eating the victim actually took the sin away

outliers.note: Alone turns the incident into a lesson about teaching, that the ablest master’s labour is fruitless without obedient scholars of retentive memory, and that God’s repetitions are not superfluous since we do not understand what we seem to understand.

19.pericope_label: And Aaron said unto Moses, Behold, this day have they offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the Lord; and such things have befallen me: and if I had eaten the sin offering to day, should it have been accepted in the sight of the Lord? And when Moses heard that, he was content.

schools.summary: Put the excuse into direct speech and call it appropriate and dignified, then turn from the case to the principle, that God has given human nature the privilege of weeping and ordained that tears should be the outlets of our sorrows; and close on the warning that he will not suffer human institutions to take the place of his own prescribed worship, while allowing that Aaron sincerely aimed at pleasing God, who is not extreme to mark what is done amiss.

Trace the shape of Aaron's excuse and find it carefully built — first that everything else that day was done in strict accordance with the ritual, then the calamity that unfitted the survivors, then the submission that eating would not have been acceptable; and read the contentment of Moses as a remarkable instance of humility and of the human side of his nature, noting the tradition that ascribes the mistake to him rather than to Aaron.

Explain why Aaron answers a charge laid against his sons, being sensible that he was pointed at and that the blame lay as much on him; and observe that the case had a real difficulty in it, the flesh of a sin offering being sometimes to be eaten and sometimes burnt, so that a first offering made the mistake easy — which may be why the goat was sought so diligently.

sides.position: Aaron's, excusable through grief and through the genuine difficulty of a first sin offering
Moses', who spoke hastily and acknowledged it — as Jewish tradition has held from time immemorial
An irregularity justified in a measure by necessity, which God did not punish and Moses did not press

outliers.note: Alone reports the Palestinian Chaldee paraphrase in which Moses sends a herald through the camp to announce that it was he from whom the law had been hid, and his brother Aaron who brought it to his remembrance.

Alone turns from the case to a theology of tears, that God has given human nature the privilege of weeping and ordained that tears should be the outlets of our sorrows and tend to exhaust the cause from which they flow.
